skill.name: webgl
skill.description: Implements or debugs raw WebGL/WebGL2 contexts, GLSL, buffers, textures, and GL draw calls. Use for direct WebGL API work, not generic 3D tasks owned by a higher-level renderer.
skill.summary: Guide raw WebGL development with context setup, resource management, shader optimization, and browser rendering diagnostics.
skill.author: shreyam1008

content.user_title: Build and Debug Raw WebGL Rendering
content.value_statement: Raw WebGL rendering can slow down through excessive draw calls, state changes, and texture bandwidth. This skill guides context setup, resource handling, and targeted optimization.
actual_capabilities: Guide WebGL2 context configuration, unavailable-context fallbacks, and context loss recovery.
Explain device pixel ratio limits, canvas sizing, and viewport synchronization.
Recommend indexed drawing, instancing, vertex array objects, and appropriate buffer usage hints.
Guide shader compilation timing, uniform caching, precision choices, and reduced fragment work.
Recommend mipmaps, compression, and texture atlases to reduce texture bandwidth and binding costs.
Guide animation scheduling, browser profiling, and avoidance of synchronous GPU readbacks.
limitations: Provides instructions and small examples, not a bundled renderer or executable profiling tool.
Focuses on raw WebGL APIs rather than complete Three.js or React Three Fiber scene graphs.
Cannot guarantee GPU selection, extension availability, browser support, or performance improvements without testing.
Experimental HTML-in-Canvas texture methods require feature detection and a supported fallback.

use_cases.title: Initialize a browser visualization
use_cases.description: Plan WebGL2 context setup, responsive canvas sizing, unavailable-context behavior, and context restoration for a custom visualization.

use_cases.title: Improve repeated-object rendering
use_cases.description: Review draw calls, state changes, buffers, and instancing for a browser game that renders many similar objects.

use_cases.title: Investigate rendering bottlenecks
use_cases.description: Use browser inspection and hardware measurements to prioritize shader, texture, and readback improvements in an existing renderer.

prompt_templates.title: Start a WebGL2 canvas
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me initialize a raw WebGL2 canvas. Include context options, device pixel ratio sizing, viewport setup, and behavior when WebGL2 is unavailable.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner: configure a first rendering context.

prompt_templates.title: Recover from context loss
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my WebGL context lifecycle: [paste relevant code]. Explain how to stop rendering, allow restoration, recreate resources, and restart safely.

prompt_templates.title: Reduce rendering overhead
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this raw WebGL rendering path: [paste code and draw call measurements]. Recommend batching, instancing, buffer reuse, and state grouping with validation steps.

prompt_templates.title: Plan measured GPU optimization
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze these target-device profiles: [paste measurements, browser versions, and renderer details]. Prioritize shader, texture, and readback changes while preserving precision and compatibility.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: compare performance tradeoffs across devices.

output_examples.input: My canvas looks blurry after resizing on a high-density display. What should I check?
output: Compare the canvas drawing buffer dimensions with its displayed dimensions.
Scale the drawing buffer by the device pixel ratio, using a cap appropriate for your performance budget.
Update the viewport whenever the drawing buffer changes.

output_examples.input: My renderer draws hundreds of copies of the same mesh and slows down. What should I inspect?
output: Count draw calls and inspect redundant program, texture, and buffer bindings.
Consider instanced drawing for repeated geometry and group objects that share rendering state.
Reuse geometry buffers and compare frame timings on target hardware before and after changes.

output_examples.input: Rendering stops after WebGL context loss. How should recovery work?
output: Prevent the default context loss event behavior to allow restoration, then stop the render loop.
Recreate GPU resources when the context is restored.
Restart rendering after resource initialization completes.

best_practices: Profile on target browsers and devices before choosing optimizations.
Keep GPU resources reusable and handle context loss before deploying.
Feature-detect optional extensions and experimental methods, then preserve a supported fallback.
anti_patterns: Recompile shaders or reallocate geometry buffers every frame without a demonstrated need.
Call synchronous GPU readback or error checks repeatedly in performance-sensitive rendering loops.
Assume a power preference hint or renderer string proves performance or guarantees a discrete GPU.

faq.question: Which AI tools support this skill?
faq.answer: The declared supported tools are Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.

faq.question: Does this skill replace a rendering library?
faq.answer: No. It provides guidance for raw WebGL APIs. Complete scene graphs are better handled by established libraries such as Three.js.

faq.question: Should I use WebGL1 or WebGL2?
faq.answer: The skill recommends WebGL2. Use WebGL1 when your browser requirements demand it, and provide a fallback when a context is unavailable.

faq.question: Can it guarantee a specific GPU?
faq.answer: No. powerPreference is only a hint. Renderer information can be unavailable for privacy reasons and does not establish performance.

faq.question: Does it include executable tools?
faq.answer: The reviewed package contains one instruction document with small browser JavaScript examples. It does not bundle scripts or an executable profiling tool.

faq.question: Is the experimental HTML-in-Canvas path required?
faq.answer: No. The skill treats it as optional and requires feature detection. Keep semantic DOM or an established texture pipeline as a fallback.
